preamble: Unrounding combined with lowering of the high front rounded vowel [y(ː)] to [e(ː)] is the hallmark of Kentish and south-eastern English. Elsewhere Old English y and ȳ (from i-mutation of u, ū) either stayed rounded (south-west, West Midlands) or unrounded to [i(ː)] (north, East Midlands). In Kentish, /y(ː)/ and /ø(ː)/ had already been replaced by /e(ː)/ by the late 9th to early 10th century. The change survives in Middle Kentish spellings such as ver 'fire' and velle 'fill'.

examples.note: The long vowel ȳ > ē. Initial voicing f- > v- is a separate south-eastern feature.
Short y > e. This is the south-eastern type, against Midland and Northern fillen.
